lesson.title: Zählen II: null, die Zahl, die Nummer, die Hälfte, die Million
lesson.subtitle: zero, and the four nouns that count for you

hook.title: Zero Is a Latecomer
hook.content: null is a Roman import: Latin nullus ('not one') walked into German through the universities and stayed. English took the same Latin word through a different door — null. Between them, German and English share one number and one nothing. The four nouns are older friends wearing Latin clothes: die Zahl counts things, die Nummer is the number you look up (a phone number, a house number — Latin numerus, and English number is the same word), die Hälfte is 'half', doubled from halb the way zweimal doubles zwei, and die Million is Italian milione — 'a great thousand', built on Latin mille — which both languages bought whole through the same Renaissance French channel. Every one of them is die feminine — and only die Zahl, like zehn, carries the Z-sound.

footnotes.title: Zahl vs Nummer
footnotes.content: Die Zahl is the count itself — die Zahl sieben, a count of seven, a number in the mathematical sense. Die Nummer is the label: meine Telefonnummer, die Hausnummer, die Zimmernummer. If you can point at it on a card, it is a Nummer. If it is an abstract quantity, it is a Zahl.

pattern.title: Counting Nouns in Sentences
pattern.content: Zero: Die Zahl ist null (the count is zero) — null is an adjective here, uninflected in the commonest readings and declined like one when it stands alone. Nouns: eine Zahl / eine Nummer / eine Million take ihre normal die-forms. Doubling: die Hälfte des Kuchens (half of the cake) — des is genitive, and halb is hiding inside. Scale: eine Million Menschen, zwei Millionen. Time: null Uhr is midnight, and the frame you already own still holds — Es ist null Uhr.
pattern.linguist_note: English dropped the num- root from 'number' and kept it in 'numeric', 'numerous'. German kept the noun and gave English the adjective. Both kept die Million intact because both bought the same Italian coinage — milione, 'a great thousand', built on Latin mille — at roughly the same moment, through the same French channel.

exercises.prompt: Zero and the counting nouns — match each phrase with its reading:
exercises.target_answer: die Zahl sieben, meine Telefonnummer, die Hälfte des Kuchens, eine Million Menschen, Die Zahl ist null
exercises.meaning: count, lookup number, half, million, zero
exercises.explanation: Zahl counts, Nummer labels. Hälfte doubles halb and takes genitive des. Million is singular with its Million Menschen.

exercises.prompt: 'Wie ist deine Telefonnummer?' — which noun is the label you can look up?
exercises.meaning: die Nummer = the number you look up
exercises.explanation: Point at it on a card and it is a Nummer — phone, house, room. Keep it abstract and it is a Zahl. Both descend from Latin numerus; English kept the root only in 'number'.

exercises.prompt: Build the German noun for 'half' (with its article) — the doubled relative of 'halb':
exercises.english_hint: halb + the -te that turns an adjective into a counted share
exercises.explanation: halb is 'half'; die Hälfte is 'the half' — the same doubling that gives zweimal from zwei and einmal from ein.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the midnight sentence: 'It is zero o'clock'
exercises.explanation: Same frame as five o'clock, same impersonal es. null is Latin nullus; the frame never notices.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "The city has one million people"
exercises.target_answer: Die Stadt hat eine Million Menschen
exercises.meaning: The city has one million people

vocab_hints.note: eine Million Menschen — singular noun, plural people, and no article on Menschen because it follows the numeral bare.

exercises.explanation: Million is Italian milione — 'a great thousand', from Latin mille — borrowed whole. After a numeral the noun stands bare: eine Million Menschen, nicht eine Million die Menschen.
exercises.idea: The city has one million people
cues: Start with "Die" and anchor "Stadt" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Say zero, and reach for the right counting noun: Zahl, Nummer, Hälfte or Million.

use_example.german: Die Hälfte von null ist null.

summary.takeaway: null is Latin nullus, die Zahl counts, die Nummer labels, die Hälfte doubles halb — and all four are die.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: how often, in one word — immer, oft, manchmal, selten, einmal.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Zählen II: null, die Zahl, die Nummer, die Hälfte, die Million (The city has one million people):
twist.target_answer: Die Stadt hat eine Million Menschen
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Die Stadt hat eine Million Menschen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Zählen II: null, die Zahl, die Nummer, die Hälfte, die Million without relying on short-term echo.

null.etymology_derivation: From Italian nulla, Latin nullus 'none' — the same Latin loan as English null. [wiktionary]

zahl.context_phrase: Die Zahl sieben ist meine Glückszahl.
zahl.context_translation: The number seven is my lucky number.
zahl.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *talō — the entry lists English tale as a cognate, the same tal-root as tell; the initial t became z. [wiktionary]

nummer.etymology_derivation: From Italian numero, from Latin numerus — the same Latin word that gives English number. [wiktionary]

hälfte.context_phrase: Ich esse nur die Hälfte des Kuchens.
hälfte.context_translation: I eat only half of the cake.
hälfte.etymology_derivation: halb + the deadjectival suffix -te — the twin of half; the entry notes the old b ↔ ft alternation was never levelled. [wiktionary]

million.context_phrase: Die Stadt hat eine Million Menschen.
million.context_translation: The city has one million people.
million.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian millione — the same Italian loan as English million. [wiktionary]

zehn.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *tehun — the twin of English ten with the classic t → z shift. [wiktionary]

hundert.context_phrase: Ein Jahr hat nicht hundert Tage.
hundert.context_translation: A year does not have a hundred days.
hundert.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaradą 'hundred-count' — the twin of English hundred. [wiktionary]

zählen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *taljaną, the causative of the tal-root — the same family as English tell and tale; the initial t became z, as in two, zwei. [wiktionary]

kuchen.context_translation: Would you like a piece of cake?
kuchen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōkô; Wiktionary names only Dutch koek — see Apfelkuchen. [wiktionary]

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin minūta — the same Latin loan as English minute. [wiktionary]

vierzig.context_phrase: Mein Vater ist vierzig Jahre alt.
vierzig.context_translation: My father is forty years old.
vierzig.etymology_derivation: vier + -zig; -zig is German's ancient -ty (Proto-Germanic *tigiwiz) — forty with t → z. [wiktionary]

geschlossen.context_phrase: Das Geschäft ist am Sonntag geschlossen.
geschlossen.context_translation: The shop is closed on Sunday.
geschlossen.etymology_derivation: Past participle of schließen (to close), from Proto-Germanic *slūtaną, to lock or shut; cognate with Dutch sluiten and English slot, which first meant the bolt or bar of a door. [wiktionary]

schloss.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sloz, ablaut to the verb schließen, meaning to close or lock; English slot and Dutch slot are cognates, the English t corresponding to German ss. [wiktionary]

schweiß.context_phrase: Nach dem Sport tropft der Schweiß.
schweiß.context_translation: After exercise, the sweat is dripping.
schweiß.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sweiz, from Proto-Germanic *swaitaz. English sweat is a listed cognate, keeping the old t where High German shifted to ß. [wiktionary]

zusammen.etymology_derivation: zu 'to' + sammen 'together', from PIE *sem- 'one': Middle English had the same compound tosamen and obsolete English sam meant together — the classic English t to German z shift sits right in zu. [wiktionary]

ausgehen.context_translation: Do you want to go out on Saturday?
ausgehen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *utgan (to go out), aus- + gehen - aus is the t-to-s twin of English out, as the old English cognate outgo shows. [wiktionary]

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Described by Walter Skeat as the primary dental affrication and spirantization of High German.
